Symphony control panel

Sign in to take the controls

One press: GitHub asks, the first time only, whether SymphonyBoard may act as you, and sends you straight back here signed in. The token GitHub issues is kept only in this browser, lasts eight hours at a time (the page renews it as you go), and reaches only the repositories SymphonyBoard is installed on, within the App’s permissions and your own access; a small stateless service turns GitHub’s one-time code into that token and keeps nothing.

Sign in with GitHub switches on once its sign-in service is running; until then, use a token below.

Use a fine-grained token instead Make one at github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new: name it, pick the repositories Symphony runs in under Repository access, and under Repository permissions set Actions to Read and write (read lists the runs, write starts a workflow), Checks to Read-only, Contents to Read and write (the read shows the board and the Claude accounts’ readings, the write merges a pull request), Issues to Read and write and Pull requests to Read and write; Metadata comes with them. Adding a Claude account also needs the organization permissions Secrets and Variables set to Read and write. Press Generate token and paste it here. The token is used for GitHub’s API from this browser only; nothing of this site ever receives it. For an organization’s repositories the organization must allow fine-grained tokens (its Settings, Third-party access, Personal access tokens). This is a GitHub token; Claude tokens are made under the Tokens tab’s + Add Token, and the page never sees one.

Board

What this is

The file STATE.md on the branch board, as the board workflow last wrote it: the claims, the open pull requests, the overlaps, the queue, the issues given to workers and the blockers, and, once the repository’s protocol draws them, the dependency charts, which this tab draws in place. Rewrite the board from the Command tab to have it read again.

Tasks

How tasks work

The open issues by the protocol’s labels. An issue labelled todo and held by nobody is free for any session or worker to claim; one a worker’s label names waits for that worker; a claim is a branch claude/N. Give an issue to a worker from its row, or ask Claude about it. Open the Task form on GitHub for the same with GitHub’s own page.

Dependencies

What the charts show and read

Each open epic’s tasks and what blocks them, drawn as a chart, with the goals above their epics: the same chart the board writes into STATE.md once the repository’s protocol is new enough to draw it, and the Board tab draws that one in place, as long as it is a chart as the board writes it (any other block there is shown as text and never drawn); until then this tab is the only place it is drawn. A task is a sub-issue of the epic on GitHub, and what blocks it is GitHub’s own blocked-by relation, both set on the issue’s page under Sub-issues and Relationships; a goal is an issue labelled goal whose sub-issues are epics. An arrow runs from the issue that blocks to the issue it blocks, dotted once the blocker is closed; a node’s shade is its state (white with a green edge todo, yellow claimed, blue in review, red blocked, grey closed, and white with a dark edge for an issue in none of those states), and an epic’s heading counts its closed tasks.

Under each chart a table says the same in words. Clicking a node, here or in the Board tab, or pressing Centre its row, opens the Tasks tab and centres that task’s row there where the task tables hold it, as the assistant’s focus does, and opens no other page; where they do not (a closed task, a blocker from outside, a row the filter hides) this tab says why, and the message line under the console says the same either way. To draw it the page reads, as you, whenever it reads the issues and whether or not this tab is open, the sub-issues of each open issue labelled epic or goal and the issues blocking each of an epic’s sub-issues, at most sixty reads a draw and none once GitHub says the token has fewer than a hundred calls left this hour, and writes nothing; it draws again whenever the issues are read again (Refresh). The chart is drawn in this browser by a copy of Mermaid the site carries, loaded only when there is a chart to draw.

Nothing to draw yet: no repository is chosen.

Pull requests

When Merge can be pressed

The open pull requests with the state of the checks on each head. Merge becomes pressable once a pull request is ready and every check has passed; it asks once more, then merges with a merge commit, which needs Contents set to Read and write on the token, and the merge closes the issue the pull request says it closes.

Pull requestTitleBranchStateChecksUpdatedActions

Checks and runs

What each one starts

The latest GitHub Actions runs: the required check, the board, the workers, the coordinator, the metrics. Start one by hand: the workers take the queue now instead of at the next six-hourly run, the board is rewritten, the checks run on the default branch, the metrics branch is written.

Workers

Where workers are kept

The registry under .github/symphony/workers/: each routine or worker in Actions is one file there, and a person’s sessions need none. Adding one opens the “Add a worker” issue; its workflow checks the answers and opens the pull request that adds the file, which joins the registry when it merges. The same form on GitHub: Add a worker.

Add a worker

Press where it runs and how its work lands, give it a name, and press Add.

More settings: model, turns, area, account

Agents

What an agent is

An agent is a set of instructions and the tools it may use, kept as a Claude Code subagent file under .claude/agents/ and listed in .github/symphony/agents.json with its purpose. Any session in the repository can hand it work by name; Run starts it in GitHub Actions on a pull request or issue, on the tokens you give it here, which is how usage is divided between review, development and testing; and coordbench and flowbench measure the same file. Import brings one in from another repository or an address by pull request, so it joins only once someone merges it.

NamePurposeWhat it doesToolsRunsFromTokens

Run an agent

Import an agent

An imported agent carries only its name, description, tools, model and colour, nothing that runs on its own; read its instructions and tools in the pull request before you merge it.

Ask Claude to do it

Ask Claude opens an issue that mentions @claude, or comments on the issue or pull request whose number you give, and the repository’s Claude workflow answers there on the repository’s own Claude token, within the turn cap the workflow sets. Queue as a task files the same words as a task for the workers and the sessions instead.

Assistant

How the assistant answers

Ask the repository’s own Claude about the board: what is claimed, what is blocked, what to take next, where something stands. It answers from GitHub Actions on the repository’s own Claude token and only reads (the page offers the box only where the repository’s workflow carries the assistant, the file .github/symphony/assistant.md on its default branch), through an issue of yours labelled assistant that the page opens once per repository (“Assistant: your login”); each question is one comment on that issue and one run of the Claude workflow, and the answer comes back here, since the page reads the issue’s comments every few seconds while it waits. The workflow answers only people with write access to the repository. When the answer names an issue, a board section or a tab, the page opens it, centres that row, filters the tables or scrolls to the section, and offers a link that opens the issue on GitHub. When the answer proposes something that changes the repository (run the workers, the board, the checks or the metrics, give a task to a worker, merge a pull request) or drafts a task or an @claude prompt, the page shows it as a button that says exactly what it does, and nothing happens until you press it; the press runs the panel’s own button for it, as you, so Claude itself never writes. A merge still asks you to confirm on the Pull requests tab, and a draft only fills the form for you to send. Claude in Chrome is not needed: the page reads Claude’s answer and does the clicking on your word.

The assistant is the Ask Claude bar at the foot of the console, on every tab, so you can ask while you look at the board, the tasks or the pull requests. Its answer opens over the tab, above the bar.

Repositories

Showing

Add a repository

A repository Symphony set up carries the topic symphony. Name one to put it on the list; name one without the topic and the page gives you the two presses that set Symphony up on it, through the App’s own install page with that repository selected. A new repository starts at github.com/new; come back with its name. Open /symphony/control/?repo=OWNER/NAME to land on one repository.

Share

Their GitHub username, or an email address: the page asks GitHub which account shows that address publicly. GitHub tells no one which Google or Microsoft account a person linked, so a private address needs their username or GitHub’s own Add people page.

1. Invite them

GitHub sends the invitation as you, and they accept it on GitHub. It needs you to administer the repository and SymphonyBoard’s Administration permission accepted on its installation; without them, Add people on GitHub does the same by hand.

2. Tell them

Each opens your own mail with a note linking the repository and the invitation; nothing goes until you press Send.

About the control panel

Your Symphony repositories from one console: the board, the queue, the workers, the checks and the pull requests, the Claude accounts, each epic’s tasks and what blocks them drawn as a chart, and a box to ask Claude. The page talks to GitHub’s API as you, from this browser, and to nothing else; the token stays in this browser. Every state here is written in words and every action is a button or a link with a name, so you and a browsing Claude read and drive it alike. Each tab has its own address: #command, #board, #tasks, #dependencies, #pulls, #runs, #workers, #ask, #tokens, #leaders, #share, #repos and #about. What it costs, against the other ways of running agents, is on the cost page.

What this page keeps and sends

In this browser: the GitHub token, until you press Forget the token. With Keep me signed in ticked, it is kept for every tab of this browser, beside the refresh token GitHub issued with it after Sign in with GitHub, with which the page renews the token after its eight hours. Unticked, the token is kept in this tab’s own storage, which the browser clears when the tab closes and brings back when it reopens or restores the tab, and the refresh token is held by the open page alone, never stored, so the renewals end once that page is gone (closed, reloaded, or replaced by another page such as the cost page) and that sign-in ends with its eight-hour token. Also kept: the names of the repositories you listed, the plan you chose on the cost page, the number of the assistant issue the page uses in each repository, one it opened or found. Sent: requests to GitHub’s API, as you, for what the page shows and does (a question to the assistant goes as a comment on that issue, and the page reads the issue’s comments every few seconds while it waits for the answer; for the Dependencies tab the page reads the sub-issues of each open epic or goal and the issues blocking each of an epic’s sub-issues, draws them in this browser with a copy of Mermaid loaded from this site only when there is a chart to draw, as it draws the board’s own charts in the Board tab, and stores nothing of them: the chart is gone with the page), and nothing to anyone else, a token you paste included, which GitHub is asked about before the page keeps it; on the Share tab, an invitation to the GitHub user you name, sent to GitHub as you, and an address you type to GitHub’s user search to find that user, while its mail buttons open Gmail, Outlook, your email app or your device’s share sheet with a note you send yourself; with Sign in with GitHub, GitHub’s one-time code to the sign-in service, which answers with the token and keeps nothing, the refresh token to the same service when the token is renewed, and a sign-in’s token once more when you press Forget the token, or sign in or paste a token GitHub accepts over it, so that GitHub revokes it. The developer receives nothing from this page. The Apps’ privacy statement, which covers it, is at /symphony/apps-privacy.html.
